title: Why Being Tested The First Day Of School Is Good News
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin reframes a widely dreaded first-day scenario—students testing the new teacher before class has even settled—as a strategic gift rather than a threat. Drawing on the logic of effective classroom management, he argues that early misbehavior gives teachers an immediate opportunity to demonstrate leadership, build buy-in, and establish a classroom identity that sticks. The article identifies six distinct benefits of being tested early: it lets the teacher show who they are, builds their own confidence by converting summer preparation into live proof, raises the class’s standards in real time, signals that this teacher is “the real deal,” sets a memorable first impression, and frees the rest of the class to focus once they see consistent follow-through. Linsin’s practical guidance is deliberately minimal—simply execute the classroom management plan already taught, calmly and without lecturing—because the method is the message. The underlying claim is that anxiety about first-day testing reveals a gap between preparation and performance; the teacher who has truly internalized their plan does not fear the test but welcomes it as the fastest path to class-wide buy-in.
points: Early testing compresses the trust-building timeline: rather than weeks of probing, a single clear follow-through on Day 1 signals to the whole class what this room expects and who this teacher is.

Linsin’s counterintuitive frame is that students test because they want credibility—they are hoping to discover a real deal teacher, and calm follow-through is the only proof that satisfies that hope.
The teacher who dreads a first-day test is, implicitly, a teacher still uncertain about their own plan; readiness converts anxiety into opportunity, turning the test into a confidence-building event.

Each of the six benefits Linsin lists flows from one root cause: the rest of the class observes what happens to the student who tests and adjusts their own behavior accordingly, making the individual consequence a whole-class lesson.

The practical prescription is radically simple—if testing occurs after the management plan is taught, follow the plan; no explanation, no lecture, no negotiation required—because adding words dilutes the signal.
quotes: Being tested is an opportunity to show your new class what kind of leader you are. It cuts to the chase and, done right (see "How" below), avoids further testing.
Early testing allows you to follow through in the way you've been thinking about, visualizing, and preparing yourself for all summer. It's living proof you can do it.
After you've followed through, the rest of your class will sit up a little straighter. They're rising in real time to the standards you're setting.
Students test because they want to know if you're the real deal or just another in a long line of all-talk, no-action teachers. Following through proves the former.
Knowing that a consistent leader is at the helm releases your class from the peer pressure, excitability, and chaos that cause misbehavior—freeing them to relax and focus.
I smile inwardly when a student tests me early in the school year because it increases buy-in speed from the entire class. They want to be part of something special and I get a chance to show them.
As for how to handle testing? If it happens after you've taught your classroom management plan—which should be within the first several minutes of the first day—then simply follow it.
